point-cloud.t: The same six customers, but with the **averages subtracted** so the cloud is centered on the origin. Distances from the center now show how **spread out** the customers are.

horizontal-spread.t: Dropping every point straight down onto the horizontal axis shows how widely usage varies. The highlighted bar spans the projections, and the **variance of usage is 3.50**.

vertical-spread.t: Projecting onto the vertical axis shows how much spend varies: the **variance of spend is 2.70**. Both columns separate customers, but each axis alone ignores that they move together.

choose-direction.t: We are not limited to the two axes. The dashed line is the direction **(1, 1) / √2**, at 45°: a **mix of usage and spend**. We can ask how spread out the customers are along it.

project-points.t: Each point is dropped perpendicularly onto the tilted line. Its **position along the line** is the dot product of the centered point with the direction.

measure-spread.t: The highlighted stretch is the spread of the projected positions: a **variance of 6.00**, far more than along either axis alone (3.50 and 2.70).

high-variance.h: HIGH VARIANCE MEANS MUCH TO KEEP
high-variance.t: Along this direction the customers differ a lot, so it carries **most of what distinguishes them**. Dropping it would erase most of the information in the data.

low-variance.h: LOW VARIANCE MEANS LITTLE TO LOSE
low-variance.t: Along **(1, −1)**, perpendicular to the first line, the projections barely differ: **variance 0.20**. Dropping this direction would lose very little.

pca-motivation.t: How the total (**6.20**) splits depends on the direction: 3.50 + 2.70 for the axes, but 6.00 + 0.20 for the tilted pair. PCA searches for the direction with the **largest share**. Variance is a proxy for information, not the same as importance.
